blocks.text: Ultrasound is a widely used, non-invasive imaging technique that shows internal structures such as tissues, organs and the fetus during pregnancy. It works on a physical principle called the piezoelectric effect, which is central to the ultrasound transducer. The transducer has a dual role: it generates ultrasound waves and detects the reflected signals from inside the body.

The word 'piezoelectric' comes from the Greek 'piezein', to press; 'electric' refers to electricity. The effect was discovered in 1880 by the French scientists Pierre Curie and Jacques Curie, who found that crystals such as quartz, tourmaline and Rochelle salt (sodium potassium tartrate) produce an electric charge when mechanical pressure is applied. Such crystals have no centre of symmetry; inside them are small regions of positive and negative charge that are normally balanced. When pressure is applied, the balance is disturbed and the charges move slightly, so an electric field appears across the surfaces: this is the direct piezoelectric effect. If an electric field is applied to the crystal instead, it changes shape a little: this is the converse piezoelectric effect (Fig 20.1).

blocks.text: The printed Figure 20.1 reads 'Led Zircoante Tianate'; the material is lead zirconate titanate (PZT), as drawn above.

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: The piezoelectric effect makes it possible to turn pressure into voltage and voltage into pressure. This is how ultrasound 'talks' to the body.
